common_name: Ingwersen's Hens and Chicks (Silver-Pink Caucasus Sempervivum)

planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this small Caucasus native resents winter wet far more than winter cold.

directions: Named for English alpine plantsman Walter Ingwersen, who introduced it from the North Caucasus, this is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking true Sempervivum species, forming tight rosettes under two inches across in soft grey-green flushed with dusty pink and covered in fine silvery down. It spreads readily by short, wiry stolons that each tip into a new miniature rosette, quickly carpeting a crevice or trough. Grow in very lean, mineral soil with excellent drainage, since the hairy foliage is prone to rot if water sits on the crown through winter. A short stalk bearing small star-shaped pink flowers appears on mature rosettes in summer before that rosette dies, as is typical of the genus.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, sharply drained mineral soil in full sun; native to rocky alpine slopes of the Caucasus between roughly 1,300 and 3,000 meters.

directions: True to its name, this species from the Northern and Southern Caucasus forms notably smaller rosettes than most Sempervivum, with hairy, bright green to red-tinged leaves packed into dense mats on stony, well-drained slopes. In summer it sends up stout, four-inch flower stalks topped with clusters of rose-purple, pale-margined star flowers, a richer color than the pale pink typical of many hardy houseleeks. Site it in a scree bed, trough, or crevice garden with coarse mineral grit so winter moisture drains away instantly, since it is far more cold-hardy than it is wet-tolerant. Division of rooted offsets in spring is the easiest and most reliable way to increase stock.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; this shrubby species needs full, uninterrupted daylight of eight or more weeks to initiate its showy flower spikes.

directions: Unlike the flat, stemless rosettes of most Echeveria grown for foliage alone, this Mexican species is a semi-sprawling, branching shrublet whose blue-green leaves are densely coated in fine silver hairs and often blushed red along the margins. From late winter into spring it produces arching, leafy flower stalks up to a foot long carrying unusually large, bright orange-red blooms with contrasting yellow stamens that are a strong hummingbird draw. Give it full sun and gritty, lean soil, since both flower color and compact habit fade in shade, and let it dry thoroughly between waterings. Over time the branching stems can sprawl to two or three feet wide, so give it more room than a typical rosette-forming echeveria.

planting.note: Divide rooted stem segments in spring and plant in gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun; the low, decumbent stems mat together quickly and benefit from a shallow, wide container.

directions: Native to the mountains of central Mexico from Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi to Jalisco, Hidalgo, and Queretaro, this low, often mat-forming succulent carries small, tight rosettes of plump, glaucous blue-grey leaves tipped in red at the ends of erect or sprawling stems that can reach eight inches long. Small white flowers flecked with tiny red spots appear in loose clusters in spring. Grow in full sun in lean, mineral soil with sharp drainage; the chunky leaves hold enough moisture that overwatering quickly leads to rot. Its spreading habit makes it well suited to shallow bowls, crevice gardens, or as a groundcover among larger rosette succulents.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Root offset rosettes or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; discovered growing wild on shady rock cliffs in Michoacan, it tolerates slightly less direct sun than most Graptopetalum.

directions: Described by Reid Moran in 1971 from material collected near Guadalajara and later found wild on cliffs at El Salto waterfall in Michoacan, this species takes its name from the five stamens in each flower rather than the ten typical of most of its relatives. It forms flat, open rosettes three to four inches wide of thick, pale yellow-grey leaves with a faint purple blush at the ends of fleshy, trailing stems. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in bright light to full sun, and let the soil dry fully between waterings, since the stems and leaves hold considerable water reserves. It pairs well with other Graptopetalum and Echeveria species in mixed succulent bowls, where its pale coloring contrasts with greener rosettes.

common_name: Gran Canaria Aeonium (Pink-Flowered Blue-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after callusing in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to light shade; intense light brings out the species' distinctive pink flush on both leaves and flowers.

directions: Endemic to Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands up to about 1,300 meters elevation, this low, sparsely branching subshrub is one of the few Aeonium species whose flowers carry a distinct pink to red tinge rather than the usual yellow. Its fairly large, spoon-shaped, bluish-green leaves develop reddish margins and an attractive pink-red tint in strong light, forming loose rosettes on slowly branching stems that rarely exceed a yard tall. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun for the best color, watering through the cool growing season and letting it rest nearly dry during summer dormancy. Its wide natural distribution on Gran Canaria makes it more adaptable to garden conditions than many single-cliff Canary Island endemics.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

common_name: La Palma Aeonium (Densely Branched Canary Island Shrublet)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to light shade; in its native cliff habitat this species grows at moderate elevation with sharp drainage and good air movement.

directions: Endemic to the island of La Palma in the Canary Islands, this small, densely branched shrublet grows to about sixteen inches tall on cliff faces at moderate elevation, staying more compact and twiggy than many of its tree-forming Aeonium relatives. Its many short branches each carry small, tidy rosettes that make the whole plant look almost shrub-like rather than succulent, an unusual growth habit within the genus. Grow in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, watering through the cooler growing months and keeping it drier during summer rest. Because of its island-endemic status in habitat, nursery-propagated cutting-grown material is strongly preferred over wild-collected stock.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining soil in full sun; established, dry-grown plants tolerate brief dips to around 0 degrees F, making this one of the hardier Mexican trailing sedums.

directions: Native to northeastern Mexico into Veracruz and Jalisco, Palmer's Sedum produces multiple slender, bending stems holding relatively large rosettes of thick, spoon-shaped, blue-grey leaves with pointed tips. In early spring it erupts in clouds of bright yellow star-shaped flowers held well above the foliage, one of the showier bloomers among trailing Mexican sedums. It mounds and spreads into broad colonies several feet wide given time, making it a popular choice for retaining walls, rock gardens, and hanging containers across Mediterranean-climate regions. Grow in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil, and note that it holds up to both heat and brief cold spells better than many similar-looking trailing succulents, provided the soil stays dry through winter.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; avoid touching the chalky leaf coating, which rubs off easily and will not regrow on that leaf.

directions: Native to Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico at elevations between about 2,100 and 2,400 meters, Chalk Fingers builds up fleshy, upright stems to a foot tall densely packed with plump, clavate, pale powder-blue leaves that give the plant a distinctive chalky, finger-like appearance. Clusters of white flowers marked with irregular red bands appear on slender branched stalks in summer, a subtler bloom than its showy foliage suggests. Grow in full sun in gritty, mineral soil with excellent drainage, and water only after the soil has dried completely, since the thick leaves store ample moisture. Its sculptural, pastel-blue form makes it a popular architectural accent in succulent bowls and dry gardens.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

common_name: Miniature Joshua Tree (Dwarf Algerian Shrubby Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant rooted branch cuttings in shallow, fast-draining soil in full sun; its naturally slow growth makes it well suited to bonsai-style pots and rock garden focal points.

directions: Native to limestone rocks of Kabylia and the Constantine region of Algeria, this slow-growing, many-branched species forms a miniature tree-like silhouette, with grayish-green leaves clustered at the tips of short, woody branches that closely mimic a scaled-down Joshua tree. Shallow roots and mats of woody stems spread slowly across rocky ground in habitat, and bright yellow, star-shaped flowers appear at the branch tips in late summer. Grow in lean, fast-draining limestone-based or standard gritty succulent soil in full sun, giving it very little supplemental water once established. Its naturally dwarfed, gnarled habit makes it a favorite container and bonsai-style specimen rather than a groundcover plant.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Root woody stem cuttings in fast-draining soil in full sun; protect from any frost, since this shrubby Mexican sedum is damaged by temperatures approaching freezing.

directions: Native to Mexico and naturalized in parts of California and Ohio, Tree Stonecrop is a shrub-like sedum whose branching, woody stems can reach three feet tall and wide in a container or warm garden, giving it a presence more like a small succulent shrub than a typical groundcover sedum. Shiny, nearly round, spoon-shaped leaves cluster at the branch tips and often blush red in winter, while bright yellow flowers open from a branched, lax cluster in late winter to early spring. Grow in full sun in fast-draining soil and water only when the soil has dried out, since it is quite drought tolerant once established. It needs protection from frost, performing best in essentially frost-free coastal or warm-winter gardens or as a container specimen moved indoors for winter.

common_name: Catalina Island Liveforever (Chalky Pink-Tipped Island Dudleya)

planting.note: Separate rooted basal offsets in spring and plant in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil on a slope; this Catalina Island endemic is very tolerant of salt spray and coastal wind.

directions: Found only on the rocks and cliffs of Santa Catalina Island off the Southern California coast, this richly branched dudleya forms clumps of chalky, blue-grey, farinose rosettes whose linear leaves develop attractive pink tips when grown in full sun with minimal water. Branched inflorescences up to a foot tall carry clusters of small, white, star-shaped flowers with rosy-marked keels in late spring, a favorite nectar source for hummingbirds. Grow in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil on a slope or in a raised bed, since standing moisture around the caudex is far more likely to kill it than drought or cold. Like most dudleyas it should never be collected from the wild; propagate only from nursery or cutting-grown stock.

planting.note: Propagate from cuttings rather than wild collection and plant in lean, fast-draining rocky soil; this Channel Islands endemic withstands strong coastal wind and salt spray.

directions: Endemic to the cliffs of four of California's Channel Islands, Greene's Liveforever forms a dense clump of fleshy, pointed-leaved rosettes on a short, apically branched caudex, with the species appearing noticeably different in leaf color and form from island to island. In late spring and summer, erect branched stalks up to sixteen inches tall carry many small, pale yellow to whitish flowers above the foliage. Grow in rocky, lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, mimicking the harsh, wind-exposed coastal bluffs where it grows wild, and withhold water during its natural summer dormancy. It propagates easily from stem cuttings, which is the recommended way to obtain this species rather than disturbing wild, trampling-sensitive populations.

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty soil in full sun; native to limestone outcrops in Coahuila and Nuevo Leon, Mexico, it is still uncommon in general cultivation.

directions: A little-grown relative of Texas Sedum, this subshrub from the limestone hills of Coahuila and Nuevo Leon in northeastern Mexico carries narrow, pointed, opposite leaves on upright to sprawling stems, a notably sharper leaf shape than the rounder-leaved Lenophyllum texanum already common in cultivation. Clusters of small yellow flowers appear in fall and winter, later in the season than most of its Crassulaceae relatives bloom. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun and allow the soil to dry fully between waterings; it is drought-tolerant and well suited to xeriscape plantings once established. Because it remains uncommon in the succulent trade, seek out specialist growers or collections rather than general garden centers.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

common_name: Turkish Hens and Chicks (Golden-Flowered Velvety Rosularia)

planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this Turkish alpine is resilient to winter wet when grown in a crevice, scree bed, or container with excellent drainage.

directions: Native to the rocky slopes of southwestern and southern Turkey, this slow-growing Sempervivum relative forms small rosettes, barely over an inch across, of fleshy, spoon-shaped, fresh green leaves softened by a light velvety coating and often edged in a delicate blush of pink. It spreads by offsets into a dense mound, and in late spring to early summer sends up short stalks topped with clusters of star-shaped, soft yellow flowers. Grow in gritty, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, treating it much like a small hardy Sempervivum in a rock garden crevice, trough, or alpine container. It is sometimes traded under the newer name Prometheum chrysanthum, but Rosularia chrysantha remains the name most commonly used by specialist nurseries.
